title: Smartphones transform prison journalism. The FCC wants to jam them
content:
For most of society, the smartphone is just an ordinary part of modern life. But inside prisons like the one in Texas where I reside, that same technology fundamentally alters the balance of information and power.

Prison officials know this well, and they’ve collaborated with Brendan Carr’s Federal Communications Commission to allow cellphone jammers in state prisons. The FCC passed the initiative last week, although it’s up to states whether to participate.

Officials, of course, claim that the effort is needed to stop incarcerated people from coordinating crimes with those on the outside using contraband cellphones. But I strongly suspect that it’s really about censorship.

For the skeptical: Does anyone think those advocating for cellphone jamming would allow every incarcerated person a video camera instead of a cellphone? We all know the answer, and, if we’re being honest with ourselves, we know why.

The smartphone, labeled illegal contraband by prison officials, allows an incarcerated individual to completely circumvent institutional control designed to prevent those in its custody from accessing modern information ecosystems and documenting abuses.

title: We sued the Pentagon again
content:
The Pentagon told a reporter that his questions would land him on its “list of people to disregard.” It’s been disregarding our Freedom of Information Act requests for the list, so this week, we sued to force it to respond. Plus, how you can fight the silencing of prison journalists, and the Trump administration tries to compel yet another reporter to reveal his sources.

Back in July, a U.S. Central Command staffer told Intercept reporter Nick Turse that his inquiries about Iranian attacks on U.S. bases across the Middle East risked putting him on an internal Defense Department “list of people to disregard.”

Naturally, Turse and Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF) Daniel Ellsberg Chair on Government Secrecy Lauren Harper immediately filed FOIAs for the list. The Pentagon ignored the requests, so we and The Intercept sued this week to force a response.

title: Judge gets First Amendment wrong in greenlighting Trump’s NYT lawsuit
content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:

New York, Nov. 19, 2026 — A federal judge today allowed parts of President Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The New York Times, its reporters, and publisher Penguin Random House to proceed. Although other claims were thrown out, U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday declined to dismiss claims that the Times defamed Trump by, according to Merryday, suggesting he and his relatives committed tax crimes.

title: Trump administration targets yet another journalist’s sources
content:
Tomorrow, a federal court in Virginia will hold a hearing in a case that offers a troubling look at just how far the Trump administration will go to attack journalists and their confidential sources.

Journalist Matthew Cole is facing a Department of Justice that seems determined to force him to reveal his confidential sources. Cole was one of several journalists behind a September 2025 New York Times article about a disastrous American military operation in North Korea during the first Trump administration, one that resulted in civilian deaths.

Just five months after the article was published, the DOJ issued a grand jury subpoena to Cole, seeking to compel him to identify his sources and testify about his reporting. Cole moved to quash the subpoena, but in July, a magistrate judge recommended that his motion be denied.

If the district judge hearing the case tomorrow adopts that recommendation, it’s very possible that Cole will have to decide between burning sources and, potentially, facing crippling fines or even jail time.

title: FPF sues Defense Department for info on media ‘blacklist’
content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:

New York, Nov. 16, 2026 — The Department of Defense is unlawfully withholding information about a media “blacklist” it has admitted to keeping internally, according to a lawsuit filed today in federal court by Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF) and The Intercept.

The plaintiffs, represented by Free Information Group, are asking the court to force the department to disclose documents related to a list of journalists it “disregards,” as described by DOD personnel.

In July, Intercept reporter Nick Turse posed several questions to U.S. Central Command about Iranian attacks on U.S. bases across the Middle East. He was told by CENTCOM staff that if his inquiries on the topic did not stop, he would be put on an existing, internal “list of people to disregard.” A U.S. official later told Turse that the DOD “had a standing order not to engage with” him.

CENTCOM has ignored Freedom of Information Act requests from both Turse and Lauren Harper, FPF’s Daniel Ellsberg chair on government secrecy, for copies of the list of journalists CENTCOM “disregards.”

title: Georgia Fort stands up for journalists
content:
Independent journalist Georgia Fort is stepping up to call attention to retaliation against reporters, including her own ongoing prosecution for covering a protest at a Minnesota church against violence by immigration enforcement officers. Plus, some advice for the next Congress to fix the broken federal transparency system.

Georgia Fort is being prosecuted in a legally dubious case for her coverage of a protest against immigration authorities at a Minnesota church in January. She’s also been the subject of secret subpoenas. Unfortunately, while the scale of the government’s campaign against her is absurd, it’s not unprecedented — across the country, journalists are facing threats, arrests, and violence for keeping the public informed.

Now, Fort is partnering with the U.S. Press Freedom Tracker, a project of Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF), as well as the Committee to Protect Journalists and Protect Democracy, on a video series highlighting the experiences of other journalists under attack and how the public’s right to know has been impacted.

title: New Congress must prioritize press freedom
content:
Dear Friend of Press Freedom:

This week’s midterm elections showed that Americans want Congress to rein in the Trump administration’s abuses — including those against the press and First Amendment. After all, crooked officials attack the press precisely because journalism interferes with whatever other nefarious plans they may have in mind. Read on for more on how you can encourage lawmakers from both parties to prioritize press freedom, as well as about other developments from an important week in the fight against censorship.

The next Congress will surely spend plenty of time investigating the Trump administration’s unconstitutional and corrupt practices when it comes to the press — as it should. But that’s not nearly enough. It also needs to pass the systemic fixes long sought by press freedom advocates. The need for these reforms has never been clearer.

sourceTitle: The Latest – Freedom of the Press Foundation

title: Government lawyers’ lies and stonewalling endanger press freedom
content:
Government lawyers during President Donald Trump’s second term have outright lied to federal judges and refused to comply with court orders in numerous cases involving journalists and the First Amendment.

That’s according to a newly updated report from nonpartisan law and policy journal Just Security. Since last year, the journal has been evaluating the state of the “presumption of regularity” — a legal doctrine under which judges assume that the executive branch of the U.S. government is following appropriate procedures and being honest about the reasons for its actions.

That presumption was probably never warranted — after all, many of the dishonest lawyers serving in the Trump administration aren’t newcomers to the federal government. Some have been around for decades. But Just Security’s report reveals that the presumption has been consistently and shockingly undermined since Trump returned to office — leading one judge to announce that the presumption had been “destroyed.”

Judges in press freedom cases should be presuming that any claims from the administration must be heavily scrutinized.

title: California goofed — badly — in poll worker guidance on photography
content:
Los Angeles, Nov. 02, 2026 — President Donald Trump has been trying to undermine trust in the integrity of elections, especially in California. Unfortunately, the state is playing right into his hands by placing a veil of secrecy over polling stations and suggesting photography is prohibited outside.

Adam Rose, deputy director of advocacy for Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF), wrote to California’s top election official explaining that Trump “has provided the public no credible reason to believe his posturing — but your office is handing him one.”

Our letter joins a growing outcry in the state from our friends, including the First Amendment Coalition, ACLU of Northern California, National Press Photographers Association, and numerous news organizations.

Please contact us if you would like further comment.

title: Espionage Act: The zombie law haunting Halloween week
content:
Dear Friend of Press Freedom,

In the spirit of Halloween, we’re calling for an end to the Espionage Act — a zombie statute that keeps popping up to drag journalists and their sources into hell. More about the act and its latest victims below. Also, the Department of Homeland Security and cops are sabotaging public records requests, and a new coalition of veteran journalists is fighting back against censorship.

The Justice Department unsealed new Espionage Act charges against former FBI Director James Comey, accusing him of leaking national defense information to the press in 2016.

Comey has a strong argument that the prosecution violates the statute of limitations, but the problems with Espionage Act prosecutions go far beyond procedural technicalities. The 1917 law’s vagueness and overbreadth have long made it the government’s weapon of choice not only for political grudges but for prosecuting whistleblowers who share important news with the press and public. Comey’s own FBI led plenty of these investigations.

sourceTitle: The Latest – Freedom of the Press Foundation

title: Get the Flock away from the press
content:
Dear Friend of Press Freedom:

Meanwhile, the Trump administration continued its multipronged censorship campaign this week, while Florida politicians did their best impression of it. And for some good news: California lawmakers passed two important pieces of press freedom and transparency legislation.

Artificial intelligence-powered camera networks operated by Flock Safety, Axon, and others are making the real-world consequences of mass surveillance impossible to ignore. Nearly every week brings a news report about how these systems are being abused to stalk romantic interests and exes, help immigration agents terrorize communities, or even spy on a children’s gymnastics room.

title: Put Flock on the chopping block
content:
Mass surveillance — the government’s indiscriminate spying on large numbers of people — often sounds abstract. Most people will never know if the government tracks their license plate, phone records, or internet browsing history. Some even think that if they’ve done nothing wrong, they have nothing to hide.

Then Flock cameras started showing up.

Artificial intelligence-powered camera networks operated by Flock Safety, Axon, and other companies are making the real-world consequences of mass surveillance impossible to ignore. Nearly every week brings a news report about how these systems are being abused to stalk potential romantic partners and exes, help immigration agents terrorize communities, or even spy on a children’s gymnastics room.

title: Florida GOP lawsuit to censor TV stations fails Sunshine State — and First Amendment
content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:

Tallahassee, Fla., Oct. 19, 2026 — The Republican Party of Florida is suing a dozen TV stations in Central Florida, seeking to block a state Democratic Party election advertisement about the Hope Florida scandal, in which $10 million of federal Medicaid funds may have been misappropriated by Gov. Ron DeSantis and his former chief of staff, James Uthmeier — as well as reporting about the grand jury proceedings referenced in the ad.

Both DeSantis and Uthmeier, who is now running for attorney general, had spent hundreds of thousands in state funds to keep the grand jury report secret until it was leaked to a South Florida broadcaster in late August. Both men admonished media outlets for reporting on the leaked material, saying it was a crime. In the lawsuit filed on Oct. 16, the state GOP also threatened broadcasters with criminal prosecution for airing the material.

title: Congressional threats to BreakThrough News are unconstitutional harassment
content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:

New York, Oct. 19, 2026 — A coalition of press freedom organizations is demanding that the House Ways and Means Committee drop its threat to serially subpoena staffers at BreakThrough News. The committee wants BreakThrough News employees to testify before Congress unless the outlet drops its First Amendment and other objections to the committee’s prior subpoenas and document demands by tomorrow.

The committee has claimed its prior correspondence was in furtherance of a tax-related probe into one of BreakThrough’s donors. But the committee and its chairman, Rep. Jason Smith, R-Mo., have accused the outlet of “anti-American rhetoric” and “messaging that mirrors hostile government propaganda.” It is citing BreakThrough’s criticisms of immigration enforcement actions and of U.S. and Israeli foreign policy as examples of such rhetoric, making clear that the probe is pure viewpoint discrimination.

title: Court delivers second stinging blow to White House press ban
content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:

New York, Oct. 14, 2026 — Judge Timothy Kelly of the U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., delivered a decisive loss to President Trump for a second time yesterday evening, extending his previous order restraining the administration from barring CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House.

Kelly’s new preliminary injunction restrains administration officials from enforcing Trump’s decision to revoke the White House “hard pass” press credentials held by employees of the three news outlets.

title: DOJ’s antitrust investigation into TV networks is nonsense
content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:

New York, Oct. 10, 2026 — The Department of Justice is investigating whether ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC, and Fox News violated federal antitrust laws when the networks briefly suspended their pooled coverage of President Donald Trump, according to The New York Times.

Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF) Chief of Advocacy Seth Stern issued the following statement:

“The investigation is nonsense. Trump may view the presidency as a business venture, but news outlets standing up for their constitutional rights has nothing to do with antitrust law, no matter what Laura Loomer says.

“Depriving Trump of the attention he craves is not a competitive harm and, in any case, antitrust law has long recognized First Amendment exceptions even when there is anticompetitive impact.

“Even more bizarre than the administration’s legal theory is that after all his ‘fake news’ rhetoric, Trump is weaponizing the DOJ to pressure the networks he calls the ‘enemy of the people’ to stay at the White House. It’s a weird way of telling the press how much he missed them.”

content:

And a new lawsuit reveals that the feds scoured journalist Tim Burke’s Google and Twitter accounts after raiding his home back in 2023 and that — as with this year’s raid of the Washington Post’s Hannah Natanson — they failed to tell the judge about the Privacy Protection Act of 1980.

title: DOJ’s secret search of journalist’s accounts omitted press law
content:
Federal agents secretly searched Florida journalist Tim Burke’s Google and Twitter accounts in 2023, a new lawsuit filed by Burke on Sept. 22 reveals. At the same time, the government failed to tell a judge who approved those searches about a federal law that specifically limits searches of journalists’ materials.

Burke is facing federal criminal charges based on his reporting exposing unaired footage, including of antisemitic remarks, by the musician Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, during a Fox News interview. After receiving a tip from a source, Burke used publicly available demo credentials to find the footage on a public, albeit difficult-to-find, website.

In May 2023, the government raided Burke’s home newsroom and seized virtually all of his electronic equipment. Prosecutors later charged him with 14 felonies, alleging conspiracy, wiretapping, and violations of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

title: These secret subpoenas are targeting journalists
content:
The government shouldn’t be able to secretly demand a journalist’s phone records without a judge or the journalist ever seeing the request. But that’s exactly what happened to Georgia Fort and Don Lemon.

Fort and Lemon, who are being criminally prosecuted in a legally dubious case for their coverage of a protest against immigration authorities at a Minnesota church, recently revealed that the government sought information from Google and their phone companies about their accounts, and asked the companies to keep the demands secret.

Unlike other recent cases relating to legal demands involving the press, the government didn’t use a search warrant or grand jury subpoena to pry into Fort’s and Lemon’s records. In fact, a federal judge had twice rejected a search warrant demanding the same information from Google that the government later sought using a different method.

Instead, Homeland Security Investigations, a component of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, went after the reporters’ YouTube account information and phone records using an administrative subpoena known as a 1509 summons.

title: White House thinks it’s above the law
content:
Dear Friend of Press Freedom:

A federal judge smacked down the White House’s media ban, but the administration seems to think complying with court orders is optional. Plus: Alongside our allies, we’re continuing the fight for real editorial independence – not some unconstitutional sham board – after a baffling capitulation from state attorneys general to David Ellison’s Paramount.

Yesterday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that President Donald Trump could not bar CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House, rejecting the administration’s argument that “national security” concerns justified the ban. But despite Kelly’s temporary restraining order, all three outlets reported hours later that they were still being blocked from entering the premises. Compliance since has been spotty at best.

title: White House defies judge who smacked down media ban
content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:

New York, Sept. 24, 2026 — Hours after Judge Timothy Kelly of the U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., delivered a resounding defeat to President Trump early this morning, restraining his administration from barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House and holding that the ban is likely unconstitutional, the administration defied the order by continuing to deny access to the networks.

Kelly held that the press met the “high bar” to show that the ban likely violated the Fifth Amendment’s protections for due process. He also rejected the administration’s argument that “national security” concerns justified the ban, noting that the news stories the administration pointed to are “routine” and that there is no precedent for applying laws prohibiting disclosure of classified information to reporters.

But after Kelly’s ruling and in spite of the temporary restraining order entered by the court, Politico, CNN, and MSNOW reported today that some of their reporters were denied access to the White House and some also had their press credentials confiscated.

The following can be attributed to Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF) Chief of Advocacy Seth Stern:

title: Pablo Torre shows why we need the PRESS Act
content:
Dear Friend of Press Freedom:

Join us at 1 p.m. ET today for a conversation about a recent court victory shutting down deportations of international students based on their speech, and learn what the decision means for journalists and their sources. But first, the government is still prosecuting, investigating, and subpoenaing reporters, even as it uses journalists’ work — like Pablo Torre’s reporting on a massive NBA scandal — to launch investigations. All the more reason we need a federal shield law.

Federal prosecutors recently opened an investigation into allegedly fraudulent payments by the Los Angeles Clippers to star player Kawhi Leonard after Torre reported on the scheme, using information from confidential sources. But as Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF) Executive Director Trevor Timm points out, while the Trump administration relied on a journalist’s legwork to find evidence of crimes, it’s still attacking journalist-source confidentiality.

That’s why it’s time to pass the PRESS Act and protect journalists from being forced to reveal their confidential sources.

title: Federal court blocks Trump administration limits on foreign journalists
content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:

New York, Sept. 15, 2026 — Late yesterday, a federal judge issued an injunction blocking the Trump administration’s efforts to impose significant visa restrictions on foreign journalists and students.

Under long-standing rules, journalists have been able to visit the United States on “I visas” and report without regular interference or scrutiny of their content. The Trump administration moved to instead require visa renewal every 240 days, a significant administrative burden and waste of taxpayer dollars that would have subjected journalists to a constitutionally chilling process that could include content review. Plaintiffs in the lawsuit include Reporters Without Borders (RSF).

As the judge observed in his ruling, “DHS did not identify a single specific national security risk associated with foreign journalists on I-visas.”
